text: Mr Chairman, I would like to address this to Minister Yaacob Ibrahim.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: For students who are already on TTFS and they get, for example, the 50% subsidy under TTFS, can they re-apply under the new criteria?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: My second question for the Minister is how much more, in terms of Budget allocation, will this increase in TTFS cost the Government?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: PA activities are headed by a grassroots adviser, who is a PAP MP, and also a prospective PAP candidate, who is also appointed as the grassroots adviser, or a previous candidate of PAP heading activities on the ground.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Are these activities not considered as political outreach?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Mr Chairman, we make a distinction between political outreach and political impact.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: All Government statutory bodies, when we execute our duties, will be serving the Government of the day to reach, to fulfil the agenda for the Government of the day.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Government of the day appoints people to help it outreach, sense the ground, respond to the ground, these are all part and parcel of Government function.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: SportSG conducts activities on the ground with the community partners.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is fulfilling the functions of the Government of the day.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Then, the Member asked, when a Statutory Board and the Government agencies do their work properly and do their work well, does it have a political impact?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Government of the day, the elected Government of the day, has to run the country and have to do its best for the citizens and to fulfil its agenda.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That is why we select people to help the Government of the day to make sure that we can connect the people and to connect the people with the Government so that we can become a more responsive society and more responsive Government.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad
text: Mr Chairman, I have a question for Minister Yaacob Ibrahim with regard to MENDAKI loans.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad
text: I presume at this time there are some who are unable to redeem the loan or pay back the loan.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad
text: Can the Minister share with us how much in terms of statistics that this is now happening?

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: We are studying it to ensure that whatever loans that we give and the rate of repayment can allow us to have a sustained programme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: I can safely say that in the last few months or at least a year or so, MENDAKI's staff have been working very hard to be able to get repayment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: We just want to make sure that the repayment rate is in such a way that we can sustain the loans that we give out and what other expenditure MENDAKI needs to make use of.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: In case something goes wrong, we have some money.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: So, we need to balance all of this.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I will end the clarifications for this phase.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Mr Chairman, having lived abroad and encountered casual racism on a regular basis, I understand how difficult it is to reach what we call race and perhaps creed blindness.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We are all different people, we have our own perspectives, but what can unite us is a common purpose, nationality and pride in our community.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As a nation in constant transition, each generation brings with it new challenges.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In the early days, you not only had inter-community tensions but also intra-community ones, too.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, our focus on a meritocratic system and also careful management of social interactions and mixing of the population has erased the most obvious fault lines.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We can, therefore, safely say that Singapore does have a multiracial, multicultural harmonious society to a point.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But despite all our efforts, fault lines do not disappear completely.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As we continue to grow as a country, become more educated, we also risk becoming more diverse and divisive.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Today, we have issues of self-radicalisation, class divides and ideological tensions to deal with.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I met a young resident earlier in the month who caught me quite off-guard.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We were trying to assist him with a difficult appeal on a family matter.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: He was well-spoken and articulate, but stridently aggressive in his view.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Despite calmly explaining to him the situation, he then said that he did not acknowledge the law of the land as he only believed in the sanctity of his own religious laws.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: On a separate matter, a grassroots leader also shared with me about his daughter's experience in what some would term as an "elite girls' school".

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They came from a middle-class background and he was shocked by the bullying that his daughter encountered from more well-to-do peers.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Another is the tension that is becoming more obvious in what can be described broadly as liberal and conservative views in our society.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: In a response to the report, the Government said that it would take steps to help facilitate opportunities for people of different backgrounds to mix and, for sensitive issues, in general, a deeper level of engagement and discussions are needed.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: On serious divides, such as race and religion, such engagements have included the Inter-Racial and Religious Confidence Circles (IRCCs), where Singaporeans can have deep discussions and ask difficult questions.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: In tackling trust divides, such engagements are very important.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: First, as it is with race and religion, awareness on class differences can take various forms, such as acknowledging differences in the use of language – basically, how they speak English, for instance – types of social norms, areas of interest and hobbies.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: Having a platform that acknowledges these differences and allows a discussion on them can be a step forward towards bridging the divide.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: Second, given that shared facilities and common areas, for example, lift lobbies and void decks, are key to improving social engagement among Singaporeans, how does the Government plan to bridge residents across the public-private property divide?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Singaporeans pride ourselves on living in a fair and just meritocracy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: However, some believe that a social divide is emerging both along race and class lines.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Government provide some broad overview of the trends?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Can MCCY share what the Government is doing to bring our people together, so as to temper the emergence of social divide?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Is there scope for us to strengthen our collaboration with VWOs to bring people together?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: As such, can MCCY provide an update on their progress?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: What can Singaporeans look forward to in the year ahead?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: What else is MCCY doing to keep Singaporeans active?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Beyond keeping Singaporeans active and healthy, sports can also bring Singaporeans together.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Sports has the ability to turn strangers into friends.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: It is, indeed, as SportSG mentioned on its website, the real social network.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I recently witnessed that potential when I toured the Woodlands Sports Complex, where many communities of sportspeople were created among residents.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Families would come to the complex and participate in different sports.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: This is not just to bond residents, but also for the whole family to exercise together.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: By exercising together, they will then have the habit of going to the stadium every Friday and, therefore, maintaining an active regime.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: To sustain such good work, it is important for MCCY to invest in community organising staff in our sports complexes, and to build up networks of residents.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Will MCCY consider expanding this programme to other sports complexes, including Yio Chu Kang Stadium, which is frequented by my residents?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Chairman, sports bring much benefits, such as helping to build self-confidence and creating a good sense of time management.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These are important traits that are beneficial to the young, especially our youths at-risk.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I have a youth, Abdul Thaslim Hajanajubudeen, who used to live in Henderson-Dawson constituency where SportCares helped turn his life around.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Five years ago, he used to hang around at the void deck at Henderson playing street soccer, sometimes causing disturbances to his fellow neighbours.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A tutor who provides free tuition and motivational talks in Henderson’s drop-in centre, We Love Learning (WeLL) Centre, encouraged Abdul Thaslim to join SportCares after seeing that he had great potential in athletics.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: He wants to turn his passion for sports into a career in the sports industry.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: He is determined to gain direct admission to a Sports Management diploma course at a polytechnic.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am sure he can do it and we, at the WeLL Centre, all wish him well.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: All these ties in with our desire to help our people live a better quality of life.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We have been investing in various sports infrastructure across the country, from soccer fields, basketball courts to swimming complexes and track and field complexes.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some of these have been built for many years and I feel that there should be a review of some of the facilities to have them upgraded, or to introduce new facilities which are more popular than they were previously.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Delta Sports Complex in my constituency is one such facility that needs upgrading.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: My Henderson-Dawson residents would be very happy and excited if Delta Sports Complex can be upgraded.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Second, we certainly see many more people exercising in the parks, at the fitness stations, at sports complexes, at gyms, taking part in various organised runs and marathons, and so on.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There are also fitness parks for the seniors but their participation can still be greatly improved.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What plans are there to get more people to lead an active lifestyle, especially since we launched a "War against Diabetes"?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What is MCCY doing to encourage sports and exercise as part of a healthy lifestyle?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I agree with my colleague, Ms Joan Pereira.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The provision of sports facilities is important, particularly in residential estates, as it allows our residents to exercise, interact with others in their community, and participate in activities that keep them healthy.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can the Ministry share what plans are in the works to set up new sports facilities?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In addition, are there plans to renovate and upgrade existing sports facilities?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I think unlocking more sports facilities within schools for use by the community would certainly reduce the need for new infrastructure to be built.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I have asked this at last year's COS, and I will ask it again: can the Ministry provide an update on the number of participating schools under the Dual-Use Scheme?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This facility is sited adjacent to our Boon Lay CC and is an excellent extension opportunity, considering the limited space and services we can offer at our CC.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I suggest for MCCY to look at three things.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: One, to renovate and refurbish the village to introduce a variety of sports and facilities to benefit the sporting enthusiasts and residents living in Boon Lay constituency and the vicinity.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Two, to integrate the facility with our Boon Lay CC to create a seamless access to both facilities, reduce duplication and synergise our efforts through co-sharing of facilities and programmes to enhance sporting excellence and recreational activities and space for our Boon Lay residents.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Three, to create an all-purpose fitness gym which can be accessible by residents for round-the-clock exercise use to maintain a healthy and active lifestyle, as we are short of a gym in Boon Lay CC and there has been strong resident feedback for one.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The former National Stadium was our nation’s primary venue for events, big and small, including the National Day Parades, and a source of national pride and connection.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Since the beginning of operations in 2014, three years after its project, however, the Sports Hub has been plagued with questions on these cornerstones.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Even as it saw the opening of the Southeast Asian (SEA) Games in 2015, and the National Day Parade (NDP) in 2016, there were well-publicised disputes over management woes, consortium disagreements and even tensions between the Government and the consortium over the NDP.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Perhaps, it is little wonder that the Floating Platform is now mooted as the primary venue of the NDP, with its redevelopment to NS Square.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mr Chairman, apart from diet control, regular physical activity and exercise are important components of a healthy lifestyle that helps to keep us physically strong and mentally sharp.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: From a national perspective, a healthier population would mean everyone spends less of our individual net income on healthcare and related treatments.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is an effective way to ensure that our critical healthcare resources are not tied up to treat preventable diseases.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe that these academies and clubs are doing well and they have been well-received by the public so far.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can MCCY provide an update on the enrolment and participation in these academics and clubs?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Are there further plans to enhance these sporting programmes to extend them to other sports and activities?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And what else does MCCY plan to do to get Singaporeans to be more active?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Since its inception, Team Nila has contributed to various sporting events and its volunteers have distinguished themselves for being professional and having a strong work ethic.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am speaking from personal experience, having interacted with many of our Team Nila volunteers.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With a strong volunteer management programme and a robust volunteer training framework, I believe that Team Nila has the potential to contribute beyond their current role and be a positive force for change within the community.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What are the new skillsets that we would like these volunteers to build on?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And how can we develop Team Nila so that it can also be a platform for community volunteer programmes?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: National athletes, even those who have won medals often, often fork out funds from their own pocket to finance training and travel costs.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Could the Government provide an update as to how athletes have benefited from this fund so far?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Corporate support for sports is a large part of the culture of many countries where sporting achievements are a hallmark of success.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can support for sporting talent extend to even supporting athletes after they have retired from competitive competition, so that they can mentor and grow the next generation of sports leaders?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To use a sporting metaphor, this will allow us to help them pass the baton to build a lasting sporting culture of indelible memories and boost strong interest in sports.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, a year ago at this very COS debate, I spoke about the sorry state of Singapore football.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: And before I get into the state of football in Singapore again, let me just explain why the sport of football is so important to our country.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Football is the most popular sport in the world and, not surprisingly, in Singapore, too.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Across the island, it is a common sight to see children of all races running around kicking footballs in void decks, open spaces and grass patches.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: The sport builds social cohesion, nurtures resilience and teaches the spirit of teamwork from a very young age.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: It is also one of the few sports that can bring a nation together, as those of us old enough to remember the Malaysia Cup days can attest to.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: There is also a significant amount of public funds that go towards supporting football in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: So, a year on, where are we exactly with football in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: The much anticipated Football Association of Singapore (FAS) elections took place in April last year and a new team was voted into the FAS Council to oversee the sport in the country.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Although many in the new Council were from the previous team that managed football in the country, they promised change and a new dawn for the sport in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, when I made my speech a year ago, Singapore was ranked 164 in the world.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I did not think at the time that we would do much worse.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: We have yet to secure a win since we beat Cambodia 1-0 in a friendly match way back in November 2016, close to 16 months ago.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: We are now ranked behind countries like Laos, Cambodia and St Grenadines.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: The results for the other age group teams are similar, if not worse.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Our national coach's contract was renewed by the interim FAS Council in the run-up to the elections last year, despite not achieving the set target of a semi-final berth at the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Football Federation Suzuki Cup in 2016.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: When his contract was renewed last year, the national coach was set a target of reaching the Asian Football Confederation Cup finals in 2019.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: This goal, too, has not been achieved as we have failed to qualify for the tournament.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, given the dismal results over the past year and a half, what kind of key performance indicators (KPIs) has SportSG set the FAS with regard the national team?

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Has the FAS set a timeline for the national coach to start delivering results?

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: And now that, for the second time, targets have not been met, what are the FAS' plans with regard the position of national coach?

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, one of the other challenges facing the new FAS Council elected last year was to revive the fortunes of the ailing S League, our professional football league, which has been plagued by low attendances.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: In November last year, six months after taking office, the newly elected FAS Council unveiled its plans for the S League and the development of football in the country.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: The new Council has decided to emphasise youth development and this is at the core of a raft of changes instituted.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, while the emphasis on youth is admirable and shows a long-term approach to the game, it does beg very obvious questions.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: One of the key challenges for the new FAS Council was to reinvigorate the S League.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: How does the Council aim to fill the seats at stadiums across the island, when untested and unknown youth players will be taking to the field?

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: If the quality of play was a major factor for fans staying away from the stadiums, how will the fielding of players who themselves are learning, entice fans to come to the stadiums?

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Another major area of concern emanating from this emphasis on youth is coaching.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Do we have the ecosystem necessary to facilitate this youth development, and to ensure that the under-23 players have what it takes to compete in the S League?

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: There was also a recent announcement by the FAS that it will partner privately-run football academies to grow the quality and pool of youth talent.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: However, the devil, they say, is in the details.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: How is the FAS going to ensure that the quality and standards it desires are achieved and that coaches have the necessary credentials?

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Most of these academies hire ad hoc part-time coaches who may have played football at a senior level but are not qualified or trained to nurture young talent.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: But the bigger and more pressing issue is this: while this emphasis on youth is good for the future, what happens to the here and now?

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Football youth development will take years – if done well with an adequate coaching set up – to achieve the kinds of standards we aspire to.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Meanwhile, World and Asian football are not going to stand still and wait for us to catch up.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: So, what can we expect for the new season of the S League that is about to kick off at the end of this month, and football, in general?

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond the emphasis on youth, one good development is the strong efforts by the FAS to stamp out smoking among footballers, particularly, the younger players.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Personally, I am baffled that it took so long for the FAS to act on this, given that any sport, not just football, should have a zero tolerance for smoking and require athletes to be in peak fitness.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Regardless, better late than never, so it is a good move on the part of the FAS.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: While the FAS has stated recently that fans should not be fair-weather fans and should show our support for the Lions, surely, we must also acknowledge that when you have had horrible "weather" for a year and a half, even the most diehard fan cannot be criticised for praying for glimpses of sunshine before turning up.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I do hope that a win for the Lions will be the beginning of a good year for Singapore football.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: And I hope very, very much that my next speech on sport will be a celebration of our football successes.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: A day later, media reports mentioned the newly-elected FAS President, Mr Lim Kia Tong, as saying "The new work starts now and my team and I promise that we will work tirelessly to heal Singapore football and bring back the glory days".

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: It has been almost a year since the new Council took office.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: To name some, the National Football Academy and Centres of Excellence, the Foreign Talent Scheme and FAS Youth Development Programme.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: So, the question again is what has gone wrong?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: I believe FAS will also have a hard time finding answers.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: One possible way to find the answer to this predicament is for FAS to conduct an in-depth study involving different stakeholders and, more importantly, to involve our national football players from the different eras of 1970s, 1980s, 1990s and the current.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: I do hope that we will be able to find the healing formula for Singapore's football soon.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Mr Chairman, having an appreciation for our shared culture and heritage as Singaporeans is key in developing a sense of national identity and pride.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: It underpins our very confidence as a nation.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: But as we experience rapid growth, it can be challenging balancing between heritage and development.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: What is most visible of heritage is seen in the buildings and our cityscape.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: It is also in our landscape and nature.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: It can be experienced in the language that we speak, the food we eat, the clothes we wear, the books we read, the traditions we follow.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: But most often, heritage is what is inside us, what makes us who we are.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: It is intangible, immaterial, but felt most keenly inside.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: The then-CEO of English Heritage Prof Simon Thurley described what is called the heritage cycle to incorporate culture and heritage into daily life.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: He describes the four-step process as, first, understanding our culture and heritage.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Only then, will we begin to value it.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: It is from valuing our heritage that we can learn to care for it and eventually find enjoyment or fulfilment from it.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: With more enjoyment, we will then want to learn and understand more.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: That is something we may consider emulating as we seek to preserve our own heritage in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Do we do enough to educate ourselves of the importance of our local heritage?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Do we value enough our heritage to do more and allow it to thrive again?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Do we find fulfilment from our culture and heritage beyond the superficial?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: In this light, can the Ministry share how it plans to safeguard, enliven and promote understanding of our heritage, so that we can develop a stronger and more rooted sense of identity in our people?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: How will the Ministry get more Singaporeans on board and be involved and interested in our heritage plan?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Mr Chairman, our heritage is our touchstone, our point of reference, a mark of identity.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: As Jackie Kennedy once said: "If we don’t care about our past, we cannot hope for the future".

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: It is also an avenue to empower the less advantaged amongst us, including the isolated elderly, people with disabilities and youths at-risk.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This vision, however, can only be achieved if we make arts accessible to the different groups within our community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This means, everyone, regardless of their social status, background and abilities, should have access to various spaces, such as museums, heritage sites, theatres, and have the opportunity to participate in arts programmes.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Also, how many more groups would the Ministry be reaching out to?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We need to continue to ensure that the arts and heritage spaces are accessible.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Has the Ministry assessed the accessibility of the different spaces for the different groups?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: How can our arts and heritage spaces be more inclusive and welcoming for people with disabilities?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: What else is the Ministry doing to ensure that the underserved and the underprivileged in our community have access to arts and heritage?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Dr Lim Wee Kiak, you have three cuts.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: The keen interest can be seen in both ticketed, as well as free events.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: The number of arts and cultural companies and arts societies has also been increasing lately.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: The data from MCCY is a useful indicator that our arts scene is, indeed, growing but, certainly, there is more to it than numbers.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: How effectively have these funds been utilised and how has this helped to develop our local arts creators?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Moving forward, what strategies will be employed to further develop our arts scene?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Can the Minister share the plans to enhance engagement and education in relation to arts, especially for youths and children?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Art enlivens our community, as well as outdoor spaces, and creates shared memories for Singapore.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Displaying art in public brings it closer to the people, eradicating the notion that art is only for a specific group of people.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: From the heartlands, places of interest, business and shopping districts to the Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) stations, it has become a common sight to see local artists and tourists whipping out their phones to take photographs, as well as people waiting by these art pieces which they have now embraced as landmarks.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: More importantly, several of all these art pieces are commissioned to local artists, making public spaces an ideal platform to gain exposure.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: The various free guided trails deserve more awareness as they are perfect opportunities to instill knowledge on heritage and culture to Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Can MCCY update on the Public Art Trust?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Are there plans to bring arts to more spaces?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: The rise of the "gig economy" brings about many exciting opportunities for freelancers who aspire to be their own boss, pick their own projects and work flexible hours.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: In reality, the situation is not always rosy for the majority.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Aside from the lack of a stable income, freelancers grapple with a myriad of legal and administrative challenges.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Last year’s results of the Graduate Employment Survey indicated that there is an increase in freelance and part-time jobs being evident among graduates from courses in the arts and humanities.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: This would largely be attributed to the nature of their work, which is mostly project-based and spans across a specific duration.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: The Government has introduced measures to help this group of freelancers.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: The gig economy is fast becoming a global trend.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: We can only expect more creative freelancers to enter the industry, whether by choice or by circumstances.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Kok Heng Leun, you have two cuts of nine minutes.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: First, I would like to declare my interest as I run a theatre company in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I would also like to take this opportunity to offer some of my insights on ACSR and some suggestions as to how its scope can be widened.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: If we ask people in the streets, their response might be our food or our language "Singlish", or our behaviour that we are "kiasu", or even our love for shopping.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Some of us would have heard from overseas friends that the Singapore culture is clean, safe, disciplined, not allowed to chew gum, we cane people, and we have little freedom of speech.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But the Singapore identity goes much deeper than that, which I am sure everyone here agrees.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The late dramatist, Kuo Pao Kun, had imagined our cultures as a tree with deep roots.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We are, first of all, a multiracial society, where different races do not live in segregation.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We practise different faiths and it is not uncommon to see different places of worship lined up next to one another.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: That is a unique symbol of our identity.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We speak different languages and use different registers with one another, often with ease.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It is encapsulated by our cultures, our memories and our social connections.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: All these come together to form a collective body that we can identify with in an instinctive way.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: So, when we talk about defining the Singapore identity in a globalised world, we should talk about our uniqueness that define us in a positive way; we should talk about our sense of belonging, our shared experiences and histories; we should talk about our loyalty, our patriotism and our emotional connection to our country, our past and our future.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But what do we really know about our past or, rather, what do we know beyond the surface − the stories of colonisation?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It is one composed of diverse players and their struggles.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But everyone’s story is equally valued, because we learn lessons from history ─ lessons of courage, of defeat, of convictions, of quests to build better lives for communities beyond oneself.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: These stories become part of the fabric of who we are, collectively, as Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Stories about Singapore's colonisation, our fight for Independence, the struggle during the 1950s and 1960s; stories about communists and ex-communists, stories about so-called Marxist conspiracies, stories about men and women incarcerated, detained without trial.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: These are stories which should be part of our national conversation.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Instead, they are often hidden and often ignored in the national narrative.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Why is the Government so averse to these narratives and dissensus?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Why are certain Singapore artworks which offer alternative or counter narratives restricted from public screening or slapped with a Restricted Artistic (RA) rating, suitable only for those 18 and above?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Why should Singaporeans, especially younger Singaporeans, be denied the multifaceted and complex histories that make up our identity?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Complexity matters because it shows how diverse we are, and also how courageous we can be in confronting ourselves ─ our achievements and our errors alike.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The diversity of our narratives needs to be validated with immediate effect.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Our people today are a mature, discerning one.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: By providing access to disparate perspectives of history, as opposed to any "official" account, we are not only acknowledging that Singaporeans can think critically, but also have every right as a citizen of this nation to do so.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: When we silence or disregard certain narratives, are we then effectively saying our people are incapable of understanding complexities, or that we do not trust them enough to do so?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: He wrote in a radio play which was performed in the 1960s. "A national history and national consciousness begin when the history of every community is accepted as part of a common Malayan history, just as in Europe, the history of the groups, tribes and states were moulded into a common national history.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It is not a question of falsifying history, but of re-examining historical facts in the light of the present.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, search the buried past ─ the stones, monuments, chronicles, folklore, language, religion, bones, names ─ all the curled, gnarled roots sunk in the soil of history.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Look at history from the standpoint of the Malayan Man, from the viewpoint of a people on the threshold of Merdeka turning to look back at the long road they have travelled.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Do this and you will see a new pattern, a meaningful pattern emerging out of the past." Because of his appreciation and involvement in the arts, Mr Rajaratnam, I believe, was a more all-rounded, astute and humane politician.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Which brings me to my next point – Arts Education.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: With active participation, people become more creative, too, but is creativity an end in itself?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I urge our arts educators to go beyond that.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We should aim for our community and students to make creative interventions.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Creative interventions mean that the people become activists of their own lives.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Rather, when people become conscientised, they become more aware of their rights, choices and decisions.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: This will definitely benefit any ruling government, because an active and informed citizenry can comprehend Government policies and implementations better.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Creative interventions steer us from viewing our world solely as a coldly pragmatic one, focused just on economic returns or efficiency.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Instead, we begin to understand our interconnectedness – people to people, people to institutions, people to environment.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Our values will then be influenced by the consideration of our shared space and based on mutual respect and dignity.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: After all, the second key ACSR focus is: promoting social cohesion amongst all segments of the population.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Is that why PA is keen to organise huge numbers of large events at their community centres?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It takes many years of support to hone an artist’s craft.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Even so, only a handful amongst artists will be able to gain international standing.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Not every artist that gets a grant will be successful but, like any research and development (R&D), the cultural capital accumulated in the process will have a long-lasting impact.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Just like what Mr Sim Wong Hoo was going through, 20 years before he got into another new innovation.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It is especially difficult for them to secure funding from private donors and corporate sponsors.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: How then can we support these artistic experimentations?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: One sustainable approach is to build the capacity of our bigger institutions like the Esplanade, Singapore Symphony Orchestra (SSO) and Singapore Chinese Orchestra (SCO).

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Develop their fundraising team so that they can obtain more corporate sponsorship.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Now, I would also like to first thank all our colleagues who have been talking about the importance of arts and culture.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: So, here, I would like to end with a plea to all politicians: please try to understand and engage with arts and culture more deeply.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Look beyond the statistics, economics, policies, deliverables and KPIs.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Behind each of these is a human story.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Your humanistic experience and profound participation in arts will make you more aware of the people you serve and also of the artists' significance in society.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: There are thousands of full-time, part-time and freelance arts educators, art students and artists in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Please come to our performances and exhibitions, literature festivals and buy Singlit.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Could the Member kindly wrap up your speech, please?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Make meaning, share your thoughts and engage with us.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: The study also found that more can be done to improve the mixing among the various socioeconomic classes, especially people with different school backgrounds.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Can MCCY provide an update on the progress of this initiative and its effectiveness at encouraging mixing among students of different backgrounds?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: The IPS study also highlighted that people who study in elite schools also tend to be less close to those in non-elite schools and vice versa.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Can we ensure that each of these OBS camps includes students from both the so-called elite and non-elite schools?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: To strengthen social cohesion, it is important that our youths interact with different groups to understand one another's views.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Hopefully, through these camps, our youths can form lifelong friendships with one another, regardless of class.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Chairman, during the Budget Debate, I spoke about getting our youths to think ASEAN.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: It is important for Singapore, especially our youths, to understand, network and integrate with other ASEAN countries, given ASEAN's rising economic force and as driver of global growth.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: It is more important than ever that our youths learn more about the region, instead of looking only at the traditional markets like the West and China.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: What are the Ministry's plans to strengthen cultural and people-to-people ties within ASEAN during Singapore's Chairmanship year?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Does MCCY plan to use this opportunity as ASEAN Chair to help integrate our youths with the ASEAN community, and to get our youths to feel more to think ASEAN?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: How can we encourage our youths to further explore the opportunities available to them in ASEAN and to experience all the cultures and experiences that ASEAN neighbours can offer?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: I also hope for our youths also get the chance to see the economic dynamism and opportunities within ASEAN.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Lastly, is there more that MCCY can do to work together with MTI and MOE, through a whole-of-Government approach, to shift our youths' mindset to think ASEAN?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Sun Xueling, you can take your two cuts together, please.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Chairman, we need forward-looking and entrepreneurial youths to flourish in the new economy.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, it is more important than ever that our youths learn more about the region.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The five tenets of entrepreneurship, employment, awareness of ASEAN, volunteerism, and leadership and resilience as well are worthy goals for any youth to aspire to.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we improve our youths' capabilities in these areas and prepare them for the future?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We need to expose our youths to the different cultures and experiences that our ASEAN neighbours have to offer.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How does the Singapore-ASEAN Youth Fund help integrate our youths further with the ASEAN community?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can we tap upon successfully implemented programmes, such as the ASEAN Youth Summit, to drive collaborative progress throughout ASEAN?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Understandably, the knowledge that a more volatile and complex economy will require skills that youths may not yet fully grasp, can present a daunting future.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But like past generations of young Singaporeans, youths strive to create a future for themselves amidst uncertainty.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the process, youths balance their ideals with the need to make pragmatic solutions, because pragmatism allows the best ways and best methods to be selected to support ideals, and idealism is needed to give meaning to the need to be pragmatic.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Chairman, I would like to inquire how MCCY plans to engage youths to support them to achieve their ideals.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Further, how do we work with them to take in their inputs on key policy issues?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we bridge gaps in evolving value systems and focus on the common traits that bind across generations?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Rahayu Mahzam, you can take your two cuts together, please.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The youths of today will be the ones helming the nation in the future.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: It is crucial to engage them and let them have a say on key issues affecting our people.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I note that the Ministry has taken a lot of effort to engage our young people.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In particular, I note that the National Youth Council (NYC) has done a lot over the years to understand youths and refine its outreach.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I am a new council member, and it has been exciting to hear about the work in this sector.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Reaching out to the diverse groups of youths can be challenging.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The youths today have very different experiences from the generations before them and aspire for different things.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: There is, therefore, a need to truly understand the group before we can harness their potential.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: There is scope to enhance such engagements by having targeted approaches for the different archetypes of youths.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Not all are vocal and not all may be interested in giving their views.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: But they should be interested, and their views matter.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We could look at sharing information and obtaining feedback in the medium that is more suitable and comfortable for the different groups.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This could mean repackaging information in bite-sized forms and engaging them through social media.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We go to them, have discussion sessions where they hang out after school or where they seek recreation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We should also be open to implement meaningful ideas generated from the discussions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I, therefore, hope the Ministry will consider providing our youths with opportunities to play a part in policy making.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This could encourage more mature and constructive discussions in the youth sphere, which will, hopefully, help to shape views and instill the youths with the same sense of responsibility and ownership of our Pioneer Generation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We say this very often, that we all have a part to play in our nation's development.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: However, we need to go beyond platitudes and think about the things that we can do to contribute to our country.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I saw it as a call to action, a platform which allows Singaporeans to take ownership of their vision for the country and do something about it.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I am, therefore, keen to find out more about the usage of this fund.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I think the usage can give a reflection of people's passion in doing various projects for the community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The data could perhaps inform us about the awareness of the fund and the different interests out there.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Perhaps we could do more to encourage more people to use the fund.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: The Singapore Government has generally maintained an arm's length relationships with charities.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Under the current framework, the Government sets the broad policies and directions and leaves it to NCSS to disburse funding and the Commissioner of Charities to police them.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Apart from a small number of charities that have the financial resources to employ a management team, most charities are volunteer-run and are supported by a small administrative team.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: It is unrealistic to expect these smaller charities to have complex management systems and be well-versed with all the regulations associated with the collection of donations.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: There is also a danger that these disingenuous individuals might take advantage of public compassion to solicit funds in the name of charity and divert those funds for non-charitable purposes.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: The problem is likely to be exacerbated by the rise of fake news and Internet scams where scammers create official-looking websites and documents to try and trick or deceive the public and donors into donating funds.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Mr Chairman, I would like to thank all the Members who have spoken on the work of MCCY.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: MCCY was formed just over five years ago at a time when we were starting to see the emergence of new fault lines and a more fractious global environment.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Today, global forces continue to pull at the fabric of societies.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Globalisation is creating wider opportunity, but also economic dislocation.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This has fuelled discontent among those left behind and a rising mood of nativism.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The Internet is offering people a broader reach, more choice over what to pay attention to and what to filter out, resulting in online echo chambers that polarise society.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We see people retreating into insular communities based on their faith, ethnicity, status or ideology.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The key challenge for us, therefore, is how we can strengthen our social fabric and solidarity in the face of these forces, so that we remain resilient in turbulent times.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Only a united Singapore can withstand the headwinds we will face in the future.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: In confronting this challenge, we will be building on strong foundations.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Over the last 50 years, we have grown a shared sense of national identity that anchors every Singaporean, so that we can stand fast in the face of change, and stride confidently into the future as a nation.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: As Dr Lim Wee Kiak noted, through our work in the arts, heritage, sports, volunteerism, youth and community sectors, we have made good progress over the years.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We grew audiences in the arts and heritage through broad-based festivals and programmes, such as the Singapore Night Festival and the Heritage Festival, as well as high-quality platforms, such as the Singapore Art Week.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Together with the SHINE Festival for youths, as well as GetActive!

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Singapore, which includes the Singapore National Games and Inclusive Sports Festival, we united our nation in celebration.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: In engaging our community and youth, we created new platforms for dialogue and interaction, such as SGfuture and BRIDGE.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We also provided support for ground-up initiatives and volunteerism through Our Singapore Fund, Harmony Fund, Youth Corps Singapore, and Company of Good so that more Singaporeans can contribute to our community.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We made significant investments in new and refurbished facilities for culture, community, youth and sports.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: These include the National Gallery Singapore, Indian Heritage Centre, Singapore Chinese Cultural Centre, National Museum of Singapore, HeartBeat@Bedok and OBS@Coney campus.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We set up the Cultural Matching Fund (CMF) and the One Team Singapore Fund (OTSF) to encourage shared ownership in growing our cultural and sports sectors.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Singaporeans' engagement in the arts, heritage and sports has grown.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Both increased from just over 40% in 2011.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Nine in 10 Singaporeans are satisfied with race and religion relations.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Well over 90% are proud to be a Singaporean and think of Singapore as their Home.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: It is about building a home we are anchored to, cared for and feel proud of.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: It is about making home a place where we can lead fulfilled lives and pursue our dreams.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: What we do goes to the heart of the nation, because home is where the heart is.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This year, MCCY will focus on partnering Singaporeans in building a home where we share memories, values and aspirations; a home where we respect, understand and trust one another; and a home where we care and look out for one another.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Our nation's diversity is growing, whether in terms of nationality, affiliation or belief.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This growing diversity can be a source of creativity, vibrancy and innovation.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: But it can only be a strength if we are united and share a common purpose that is bigger than our differences.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Binding a diverse nation means emphasising shared identities we have across colour, creed or class lines, based on our shared heritage, values and aspirations for the future.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Through the arts and heritage, we celebrate our diversity by understanding where we come from, appreciating who we are and our place in the world.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Mr Kok Heng Leun spoke about the need to take stock of what we have achieved under ACSR and our plans going forward.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We have made significant achievements under ACSR in developing an arts and culture landscape which has brought more value to Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: But we do not intend to rest on our laurels and will continue to enhance our efforts through sectoral plans for the performing arts, literary and visual arts.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Parliamentary Secretary Baey Yam Keng will share more about these plans.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Mr Kok Heng Leun and Mr Alex Yam asked how we are safeguarding our heritage to strengthen our identity.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Over the past two years, we have reached out to 34,000 Singaporeans from all walks of life for their views on our heritage plans.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We are heartened by the widespread support for the Heritage Plan and its four themes of work: Our Places, Our Cultures, Our Treasures and Our Communities.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Under Our Places, we will develop strategies to better preserve our tangible heritage, to ensure we balance heritage considerations in development plans at an early stage.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We will also enhance measures to better safeguard Our Cultures, our traditions, rituals, festivals and food that make up our intangible cultural heritage.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: They are the thread of continuity that connects our present to the past, and that must be safeguarded and extended into the future.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: As part of Our Treasures, we will showcase more museum collections and exhibitions that resonate with our people and encourage a strong museum-going culture.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: These three themes will be supported by enhanced digital touchpoints, more ground-up heritage projects and expanded outreach to Our Communities.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: As a member state, we will work towards listing an element on the UNESCO Representative List.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: In the coming months, we will continue our conversations with the community to uncover the intangibles that resonate with Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Senior Minister of State Sim Ann and Parliamentary Secretary Baey Yam Keng will lead some of these engagements.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We will share more details at the Singapore Heritage Festival next month.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Knowing what we have in common is not enough to build a strong society.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We also need to have meaningful interactions with one another, especially with those different from us.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: People naturally gravitate towards those who share the same background, convictions or opinions.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Mr Faisal Manap, and earlier Ms Jessica Tan and Mr Amrin Amin spoke about the recent Study on Social Capital in Singapore by IPS on concerns of a growing class divide.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Contrary to what some may assume, inequality has reduced in Singapore, more so if Government transfers are included.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: In his reply to a recent Parliamentary Question (PQ), the Prime Minister shared that Singapore's Gini coefficient has fallen over a 10-year period.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: IPS studied the diversity of our social networks and whether we were mixing with people different from ourselves.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: It found that people tend to have networks with people of similar school background and type of housing.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We connect with people whom we went to school with, and those who move in the same social circles.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Importantly, the study also found that respondents were able to name people in occupations ranging from low to medium to high status and prestige.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Most Singaporeans also had friends who were of a different race or religion.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Many respondents and their neighbours helped one another with house matters.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Singaporeans are meeting and making friends with people from different walks of life.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Mr Alex Yam and Mr Henry Kwek highlighted the importance of social mixing as our society becomes more diverse.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: There will be fault lines in any society.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: What matters is that we do not let that divide us, and we grow the common spaces where we encounter and connect with one another.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: A key finding of the IPS study was that participation in sports, arts and volunteer activities, in addition to schools and workplaces, promotes social interaction and integration across groups, and these are precisely the areas where MCCY has been working hard at to nurture social cohesion.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: At MCCY, we will continue to expand the common space for interactions and shared experiences across different social groups, through honest dialogues, shared spaces and inclusive programmes.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We are a nation that prides itself on its racial and religious diversity.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Singaporeans are willing to accept differences in cultural and religious beliefs, views and practices, even though they may not agree with them.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Yet, many Singaporeans still feel uncomfortable discussing issues related to race and religion, for fear of causing offence.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Such inhibitions can breed ignorance which, in turn, can fuel prejudices and divides in our society.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Since its launch, we have reached out to over 5,000 participants ranging from religious and community leaders to youths and working professionals.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: One example is "Ask Me Anything", a series of conferences to deepen understanding of specific religions amongst believers of other faiths.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Participants asked questions about Islam, which were addressed in small group settings and panel discussions.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The conference provided a platform for healthy dialogue, where questions were civilly raised and honestly answered.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: It proved that we can have honest, healthy and frank discussions on matters of faith.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Our focus for the coming year is to ensure that we grow and sustain this culture where Singaporeans engage one another on sensitive topics.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: To do so, we will scale up projects that have the potential to reach wider audiences and also expand outreach through social media.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: For instance, riding on the success of Ask Me Anything (Islam) series, we have brought in more partners, in collaboration with religious organisations, to run the Ask Me Anything (Buddhism) Series, and the Ask Me Anything (Christianity) series.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Our partners on the Ask Me Anything series will also produce online content, such as articles and videos related to the conferences, so that information can be shared with those who did not attend the events.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: By bridging potential tensions and social divides within Singapore, we stand a better chance in combating the threat of terrorism.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: These efforts will strengthen cohesion, trust and resilience in peacetime so that, collectively, we are able to protect our communities and bounce back in a crisis.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Going forward, we will deepen our engagement and build stronger ties with these religious organisations, as well as expand our outreach to the wider religious community.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: As Ms Rahayu Mahzam and Ms Sun Xueling emphasised, it is important to engage our youths on key policy issues.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: They will be the ones bringing Singapore forward.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: They have much to give to the here and now.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Our surveys show that our youths are proud to be Singaporean and are committed to the country.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Through conversation and dialogue, we hope that our youths will be informed on important issues, listen to one another’s views, negotiate differences and find new solutions together and with the Government.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: How will the Youth Conversations be different from previous consultations?

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: First, we will be sharing more policy thoughts and considerations with our youths.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We will listen more to understand our youths' views, concerns and aspirations.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We will provide more support for our youths in generating and implementing their ideas.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: For a start, my Ministry will work with fellow Government agencies to identify areas of interest to our youths.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Whether it is about protecting our environment or creating job opportunities in the future economy, we want to address important issues that are on the minds of our youths.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We will also invite youths to propose topics that they would like to discuss and be engaged on.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Second, we are experimenting with different and novel modes of engagement.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Participants can expect the conversations to be more candid and interactive.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This will be a platform where youths meet not just like-minded peers but also make new friends who may come from different backgrounds and hold different beliefs and perspectives.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: For example, just last month, we brought together 38 youths from different schools and IHLs to participate in Project Hope and Home.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: In small groups, youths shared candidly about what “hope and home” meant to them and came up with ideas on how to build a better Singapore.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The intimate setting provided a safe space for these youths, some of whom may be more reserved to have deeper conversations on their hopes and aspirations.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: At the end of the session, through the task of putting up a short skit, 18-year-old Asri Aziz and his group discovered that they share a common vision of strengthening community bonds and celebrating multiculturalism.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: They showed fellow participants how our hawker centres provide a common space for people from all walks of life to share food and create shared experiences.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: After the event, Asri said, “I realised that there are other youths just like me, who dream for a better Singapore together.” We will continue to try different methods of engagement, such as hackathons and Citizen’s Jury.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Youths can also learn ways of crowdsourcing and co-creating ideas with the community.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Aside from face-to-face conversations, we are also bringing these conversations online.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Dialogue is a good way to bring people together.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Just as Mr Henry Kwek shared earlier, sport has been a powerful platform for social mixing.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Eight in 10 Singaporeans agree that sport has provided an ideal platform for them to socialise with people of a different background.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Today, our ActiveSG Sports Centres work with the grassroots organisations to co-create sporting activities for the community.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: I am glad to hear that Mr Henry Kwek endorses our ActiveSG programmes and I assure him that we will be enhancing the programme at our sporting spaces.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We hope to sustain this momentum with our ActiveSG Academies and Clubs.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Mr Henry Kwek and Mr Darryl David asked about the status and future plans of the Academies and Clubs.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Besides offering affordable and structured programmes for our children, they also bring families, neighbours and sports enthusiasts from all backgrounds together.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Take the ActiveSG Football Academy (AFA) Dads, for example.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This group of fathers, in their 30s to 50s, meets regularly while accompanying their children for classes at the ActiveSG Football Academy at Bedok.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: They come from different backgrounds – real estate agents, drivers, business owners, civil servants – but their love for football connected them.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: They formed a team of their own representing the Bedok Sports Centre and started playing together.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We now have six teams in Bedok, Woodlands, Clementi, Tampines, Serangoon and Jurong East.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Another initiative, launched in 2016, is GetActive!, a nationwide sporting event that unites Singaporeans in celebration of our nation’s birthday.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Singapore 2018, we will expand the footprint and bring the celebrations even closer to the community.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The biennial Singapore National Games will return and will incorporate the National Para Games, which will be the largest national para sports competition.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We will partner the Singapore Disability Sports Council (SDSC) to introduce more para and adaptive sports events.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Under the Sports Facilities Master Plan, we will enhance and expand sporting access to Singaporeans through an extensive network of sporting spaces across the country.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Mr Melvin Yong asked about the progress on this front.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: At the regional and town levels, we have opened sports centres at Our Tampines Hub and HeartBeat@Bedok.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: In the next few years, a new integrated sports and community hub in Sembawang will be ready.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We also have new facilities lined up, including new playfields at Yan Kit and Jurong Lake.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The latter will be our first "sport-in-the-park" collaboration with the National Parks Board (NParks).

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Through our Sports-in-Precinct programme and Dual-Use Scheme, we continue to roll out accessible play spaces and facilities closer to our neighbourhoods.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Ms Joan Pereira and Mr Melvin Yong spoke about upgrading the older sports complexes.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: SportSG is rejuvenating our existing public sports facilities in phases under the Master Plan to cater to increasing demand and ensure greater accessibility to our existing sports centres.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This year, we will see the rejuvenation of a few sports centres, such as those in Delta and Choa Chu Kang.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: SportSG will also work with Boon Lay CC on sharing facilities and programmes to enhance sporting experiences for residents.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Ms Sylvia Lim asked about the Sports Hub.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The Sports Hub is a place where memories as a nation is made, where Singaporeans can come together to enjoy a wide range of sports, lifestyle and entertainment events, celebrate our National Day and cheer on Team Singapore like we did at the SEA Games and ASEAN Para Games in 2015.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: It is also an important training venue for many of our National Sports Associations (NSAs).

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The Sports Hub has seen a steady increase in its visitor traffic since opening in 2014.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Last year, it welcomed about 1.4 million visitors attending over 200 events across its venues, an increase from about 1.2 million visitors attending over 180 events in 2016.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This year, it will continue to host major sporting events like the Hong Kong and Shanghai Banking Corporation (HSBC) Singapore Rugby Sevens, the International Champions Cup and the National Schools’ Games.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: An ASEAN e-Sports tournament will also be held at the Sports Hub for the first time, in conjunction with GetActive!

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: These events will take place alongside the regular community programming, such as the quarterly Sports Hub Community Play Days and free Learn-to-Play Programmes.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Like many Singaporeans and like Ms Sylvia Lim, we have high expectations for the Sports Hub, and we share the view that the operator SportsHub Pte Ltd (SHPL) can do more to enhance the vibrancy of the project.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: SportSG is closely monitoring the operator’s performance and is in regular communication with its top management to ensure that we realise the value of the Sports Hub for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: In his Budget Statement, Minister Heng Swee Keat highlighted that one of the major shifts we will see in the coming decade is ageing.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Going beyond healthcare to health, Active Health will be a journey that we embark on together for health and wellness through sports.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Just as sports can bring communities together, it takes a community to nurture healthy, active and engaged individuals who will live better through sports.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Staying healthy is more than having a first-class national healthcare system.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: It is about having family, friends, colleagues and community organisations joining efforts to support one another stay healthy.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Members may have heard of Mr Joseph Chen’s Active Health journey.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Over three months ago, 27-year-old Joseph visited his general practitioner (GP) because of a cold.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Concerned by his blood pressure readings, the doctor referred him to the Active Health Lab.
